utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, The Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, very much. Could we have appearances starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Good afternoon Mr. President, good afternoon, Your Honours. Dan Saxon for the Prosecution together with my colleagues Ann Sutherland and Ms. Carmela Javier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much and for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Appearing on behalf of the Defence today are Daniela Tasic, Chad Mair, Milos Androvic, Eaoadin O'Brien, Tina Drolec, Novak Lukic and I'm Gregor Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Madam Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The response in relation to the objection that was raised by the Defence yesterday at page 937 of the transcript lines 9 to 12, if I understand the objection it was that the translation is now going to interpreted by the witness. And that's not the case, Your Honour. Mr. Treanor said in his evidence at page 938 that he doesn't use the translations. He uses the original documents. And so there's no basis for the objection, in our view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I think it the situation that we're in at the present moment presents a number of distinct issues, the first one being that we all have been supplied an English translation either official or unofficial of a document that is originally in B/C/S. And to the extent that we all are relying on that document with regard to the examination that is occurring here, the fact that we have documents that are not officially translated creates one distinct problem; and I was fortunate enough after yesterday's session to receive from the registrar what I would call a practice directive with regard to the issue of draft translations, and I think that with regard to all documents that are alluded to in Mr. Treanor's report that are not official translations at this time we would suggest, that as to those documents, they be marked for identification, pending a final official translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me try to highlight what is a problem for the Bench. What is a problem for the Bench, Madam Sutherland, is that, first of all, we have a translation that is not an official CLSS translation. Secondly, we have the witness saying he is not relying on that translation because he has got a very good working knowledge of B/C/S. He is looking at the original document. And he doesn't rely on the translations because these translations at times have inaccuracies. The problem here is that the Defence is relying on the English version, which is he is not using, which the witness is not using and the Defence and the Bench doesn't know whether they are inaccuracies in this particular English translation or not. Now, to the extent that the witness comments on the B/C/S version and not on that English translation, to that extent, is -- you see, all along with us who don't know B/C/S, and there is no way of checking whether what he is telling is what we have before us in the English. That is my problem. And how do we finally -- because finally when we write the judgement we're not going look at the B/C/S because we don't know B/C/S. We're going to look at this English translation, which he is not using.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, you -- you say there is no way of checking whether what he is telling is what we have before us in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You can see from -- from reading the transcript as to what Mr. Treanor says and what the English translation says. And there may or may not be differences between those two. But the Prosecution has no problem in marking the documents, as -- as the Defence have suggested that any documents that are referred to in Mr. Treanor's report get marked for MFI until we have an official translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You see, if the -- the fact that the Defence is saying they will be marked for MFI is one matter. But the Bench has a fundamental problem here, whether or not, finally, that piece of evidence is going -- those documents are going to be admitted is what -- what worries us because we don't know whether that translation is correct or not correct, and we don't know whether the comments that the witness made are made on that English translation with its nuances and idiom or is it making them on the nuance and the idiom of the B/C/S, we really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Treanor has said he is expressing facts and his opinions based on the B/C/S document. Now, if we mark all the documents that are cited in his report for identification and get an official CLSS translation, then I don't -- I don't see -- I don't see the issue. If Mr. Treanor still testifies to the documents, as he has read them, he doesn't rely on the translations, and so then what you have in evidence at the end of the day is the official translation. So he is not basing any of his opinions on a draft translation or a final translation because he reads the language, and he has done for 35 years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you undertaking to go give us an official translation at some stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Your Honour. That's what -- what the Defence proposed and we agreed with that he we would marked for identification the documents that are referred to his report and get an official translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Indiscernible] Mr. Guy-Smith, and to the extent that the cross-examination and the questions by the Judges may be misguided by the English translation is of no concern.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That is of concern, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And we working now here on this English version -- the cross-examination and the questions by the Judges can only be based on the English version, which he is not going by.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could Your Honour just give me a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay, while you take the moment, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, after I made my introductory remarks with regard to the first issue I was going to proceed to what my underlying concern was, and I would say based upon the colloque that just occurred between you and Madam Sutherland, that's correct, which is that both my cross-examination of this witness; and any questions that the Chamber may pose to this witness may be misguided by the English translation, and it is of great concern to me at this time. And I think that it is of some importance that we recognise that, in fact, the witness has testified, and I refer the Chamber to -- and counsel to page 913 and 914 of yesterday's session, page 913 starting at line 25, when he was discussing the categories and the methodology that he used, he says: "When I'm asked to produce a report, I go into my collection of summaries and notes on documents most of which are embodied in a CaseMap format. I put many documents in there myself and others put under my direction, so I have all that available to me when dealing with a specific request for a report." As I understand what this means and I may be wrong but what I understand that that means is the gentleman who reads the original language then makes summaries and notes, and I don't know if those summaries and notes are made in English or in the original language. That's information that we do not have. That would be, I submit to the Chamber, information that would be the working notes of an expert by which we could all understand the methodology and the analysis and the interpretation the expert made, and that information is the information upon which he relies and apparently the information upon which he relied in drafting this report. So we are in fact, unfortunately, even a further step removed from having an understanding of the actual source information that was used by this gentleman in making his report. Not only do we have the specific difficulty that the Chamber has raised but we have a secondary difficulty, which is that the working notes that exist for the purposes of creating this report upon request, are not within the possession of either the Chamber or the Defence, which constitutes, I think, not only a potential secondary translation problem but also constitutes a problem with regard to access of appropriate information so that the proper preparation that would go into the examination of an expert can be made and considering that methodologies that is a question that has been raised here already and is obviously a question that is of some concern, we are, once again -- or not once again we are, in another fashion foreclosed from really being in a position to appropriately cross-examine or pose questions to this witness that are in fact not misguided but, rather, are questions that deal directly with the materials that he relied upon and which form the basis of his report. So I'm concerned -- I'm concerned about both the issue that -- that you have raised specifically with regard to the fact that we're not, quite frankly, living on the same plain in terms of this particular witness. We're relying on different information, in order to reach an understanding of a particular and focussed fact or interpretation of facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And as a ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And if I might, if one were dealing with, for example, examination of an expert with regard to ballistics and had in one's possession the report of such an expert, it would be expected that the underlying information upon which that expert relied, in order to form the basis of his or her report, would be supplied to those parties who are either in an adversarial position or in a fact-finding position, as the Tribunal, for purposes of being able to objectively and intelligently address the areas that are contained in the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, is that what is normally done or that underlying information is it not footnoted but invariably it's in a language that everyone can understand and you can go and read it there, but it is not necessarily supplied to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I think both of those situations have occurred when dealing with someone -- an expert's working notes, and here the working notes are the summaries -- are the summaries as he has discussed it his collection of summaries and notes. It would be something that would be supplied. Because he is -- he is -- he is potentially in a -- interpretive area based upon, if we can for the moment, value-neutral information. And part of the reason that this becomes of some importance or of great importance for an examiner is so that we can make a determination as to whether or not the methodology that was -- that was used can produce the result in a similar fashion. It's kind of a fundamental scientific concept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah. But you're going too far to.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My question is the underlying information on which an expert relies to give his report is usually not in supplied, and it is generally just footnoted and it gives references to his sources; and it's up to the reader to then consult those sources to see whether the methodology that is being used in the report is what other experts in the field do use.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Or are you saying that in this Tribunal here, even those underlying documents are disclosed to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm saying specifically in response to your first question, yes, those documents that are footnoted become available to me for purposes of examination to do precisely what you said. In addition --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But are they availed by the person who called the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's -- in addition, at this Tribunal, because that's the one question you've asked that I can be very specific about, and it's a matter that actually I had some discussion with the Prosecution today; in this Tribunal, I have not received the working notes of an expert because they were destroyed. But, had they not been destroyed, those working notes would have been supplied to us with regard to that particular expert's report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I was having a problem with --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sorry. So the direct answer to your question is, no I have not received that information. The explanation for why I had not received that information in a particular case in this Tribunal was because the information we were seeking had been destroyed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're talking about a particular case. Is it practice in this Tribunal that the underlying documents have been availed to --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I don't believe I can answer the question intelligently . I can answer the question anecdotally, and the anecdotal information I can give you is that I have been informed by my opponents and colleagues that they have not been in the practice of giving out this information, but then again I don't know whether or not the information was sought by the Defence or not. Your Honour, so I can't answer the question in -- in that particular fashion or in a fashion that is satisfactory to the Chamber. I'm more than happy to go and do the research to find out whether or not Defence counsel has asked for the underlying information and has been accepted or denied. That I can't answer. I really can't. I don't have the answer to that particular question. And I if did, I would give it to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, I would like to request from you an account of your own experiences with the previous report you had submitted in this Tribunal in other instances, as to the way you structured the report and the notes and whatever elements you want to give to the Chamber. We have been discussing here the sources, you know, the availability of the sources, the notes, the availability of the notes, by which you prepared a report and so on. We would like to get from you reflections on the way you had the structure of this report and so to help the Chamber to decide the issue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The previous reports that I submitted were written before we had CaseMap available to us in this institution. Therefore, the procedure that I adopted was to work directly from the documents in writing the report, the quote/unquote report, whichever one it was, usual grew, took shape over the course of years. The information embodied in new documents is -- new documents as they were looked at were gradually integrated into an analytical product without intervening notes since we had the documents available, and I would mark up, highlight, that sort of thing, in the documents, which is, if I may say a different procedure than the one I was familiar with going back to my days as a student 30, 35 years ago where one took notes from documents. There would be the document in an archive, and you would go to the archive take notes, or the library, take notes, return to your desk and write up your analytical product on the basis of your notes. People have written books about how to take notes so that was an integral part of that methodology. There got to be a point in time where photocopies got to be cheap enough that even students could afford photocopies, so sometimes you were actually able to get a copy of the document, that particular important document. But that is not the methodology I used here. As I said, I worked directly from the documents, and the documents are available of course on Zy. And so that was the way those reports were written. There weren't any meaningful notes. There was a -- a draft, I suppose you call it that grew over the years, and when a report was requested, then that draft would be finalised for the purposes of the given report. Now, since we have CaseMap, which is a tool we -- within OTP at least have been encouraged to use. It is possible to return, if you will, to making notes but much more sophisticated notes than was possible within the old days because it a database you can use it to search and sort and filter, and you can make links to the documents, so you can go directly from your notes to the document and have hard copy. So rather than continue putting things into an expanding draft of a report that may never be asked for or who know what is the topic of the report will be asked for is, I proceeded to put things into -- things being documents, in CaseMap; and that's where they reside. My general practice is to, or frequent practice, is to attempt to locate a translation of the document and if it's a short document, simply cut and paste the whole thing into the CaseMap. If it is a longer portion, I will select certain portions and cut and paste those into the CaseMap and perhaps summarize them. If they are translations, because some of the documents are in English, I go through those, read through them the first time around and spot any areas where I think there may be problems with the translation and again look at the document because I have it available to me in order to make my notes, if you will, and CaseMap is accurate as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When it comes to producing a report, Your Honour, I would then, if necessary, go back to the original documents and if I'm going to quote any particular portion go back to the original document and look at what the original says and not rely on my notes in that respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Sutherland, given your concession that it is of concern, if -- it is of concern if the cross-examination and the questioned by the Bench would be misguided because we would be relying on a version that it is not used by the witness what then do you then suggest as a way forward.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may just clarify. I said a moment ago that the Prosecution agreed that the documents that were cited in Mr. Treanor's report could be MFI and then we would be producing an official translation. I misunderstood the conversation, the agreement that was -- had before we entered court this afternoon and that is that we would have the documents MFI and only ask for an official translation if there were any problems raised by the Defence or any -- any other issues and not that we would be submitting an official translation of every single document that is cited in the report. And I think that -- that the parties, both the Defence, Prosecution and Bench, have to work on the translation that we have because of the problems that have been discussed before and at the pre-trial -- the trial management conference. And subsequent to the trial management conversation there were instructions actually from the Chamber in regard to the translation of documents. And if I can read that to you, Your Honour, it said that: "If the tendering party provides a draft translation of a document which has not been officially translated by CLSS, the Chamber allows the use of such a translation in Court provided that is promised that an official translation will be given at a later stage if all parties are in agreement with the correctness of the draft translation, the Chamber may consider the draft translation as the final." And so unless any issues arise, the Prosecution submits that we should be able to have admitted into evidence the draft translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand that. You haven't answered the concern I raised with you. The concern I raised with you is that notwithstanding what is written there and that is something suggested that could be used, it was suggested by registry. You will see it is not in the guidelines. It is a separate document. It's not in the guidelines generated by the Chamber, the lacuna in that is that here parties are not agreed about the translation, the witness says he is not relying on that translation, the Defence and the Bench are going to rely on that translation which the witness is not using because is he looking at the original document and coming in with his own translation and giving us his opinions based on that; and the underlying danger is that most of the time we will be talking at cross-purposes, we will not be on the same page as the witness. My question is: How is that time being put to good use if there is the danger that, in fact, this witness might be recalled later when once we've got the correct translation, and he maybe have to be cross-examined again.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: But that's the point, Your Honour, until something's identified as being incorrect, the -- the parties have to assume that the draft translation is sufficient. And we have -- we know of nothing at the moment in relation to the -- the two documents that have been used by Mr. Treanor yesterday, the Defence haven't identified translation errors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. But you note, I said to you earlier we're not working from the same page. The witness is working from a B/C/S version, which he interprets the way he does, which is not necessarily the way it is interpreted on the translation; and the translation is going to be the basis of the questions by the Defence and the Bench. This is my problem, that here and now, we are -- not going to be on the same page as we speak to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well, the Defence -- the Defence can obviously cross-examine Dr. Treanor on why he may or may not agree with the translation. But if there is an material problem, a problem with the translation going to a material issue, then it's at that point that we would seek to have a final translation, an official CLSS translation. And there would be no further examination on that document and the witness can be recalled. As you know, it's -- Mr. Treanor is within the building. It's not an inconvenience to have him recalled, if there are -- if there are problems with translations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's not conflate two different issues. An official CLSS translation is going to be required that is for sure now. Because even based on that guideline you read, that, this draft translation will become final if the two parties were ad idem about it. You are not, hence, this objection that we are having. So where -- in a situation where the parties are not agreed, then it's got, you have to get that CLSS -- let me find out from Mr. Guy-Smith. You heard what your colleague has said, if you can just limit yourself to what she said now. How do you want to resolve this issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I have been thinking about it all night, Your Honour, and trying to figure out a way of resolving the issue and moving forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: As I see it we can either MFI and come back later with an official translation and then can you check whether you did things correctly or were you misled by the translation you were using; or if you feel that your cross-examination may not be as intelligent as it ought to be if you're not on the same page with the witness that is another option. You can suggest what you think should be done in that situation. Or you may agree with translation and then it's taken as final. Those are the three options as I see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think that takes care of one of the -- one of the issues that has been presented to us. But I -- I share the same discomfort that's been voiced, that since he is operating -- and when I say this I mean no disrespect to him whatsoever he is operating in his own isolated universe with regard to how he is calling information and translating information. I have no way at the present time of knowing whether or not I am on the same page irrespective of the accuracy of the English translation that I have, which is why I had the one thought I had come up with, was that we be supplied with the information that he indicated that he used on page 913 and 914 of yesterday's transcript; and perhaps armed with that information, I would be in a position to be on the same page as the witness. I would know what he's basing his report on. That's what I come up with as a potential solution, a solution to an intelligent cross-examination, and intelligently dealing with the issue. I don't know whether or not that is of assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's the problem you postulated. At the moment, I'm asking you to make a submission as to how this impasse should be resolved. Do you want -- what do you want? Do you want to carry on with this witness and see how the situation can be remedied at a later stage; do you want this witness to be called when you are -- have you been given what you think you're entitled to?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I -- my general tendency would be the latter, to have a witness called when I have been given what I'm entitled to; but could I take a moment to confer with counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps I could say something in the interval, Your Honour. I may be able to suggest a way forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Actually, we're in the way of resolving the objection. Usually during that time, the witness is asked to remain out of it. But yes you were asked to say something by the Judge earlier, because he wanted to get something from you. Really, at this stage, you are supposed to be out of it, until a ruling is made.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I want to tread very carefully here, because I think it is of relatively major importance to my client. I'm looking at page 16 and specifically at lines 16 through 23, which is where I think I -- you posed to me what my -- what you perceived -- I'm sorry. I apologise, it's page 15. Where the options lie. With regard to the second issue, which is at line 19, that if I feel my cross-examination may not be intelligent as it ought to be, if I'm not on the same page as the witness, that is what my concern is right now. We could proceed with the witness's testimony, and at the conclusion of his testimony, if I could be afforded an opportunity to make a determination of whether or not it would be appropriate to proceed at that point with cross-examination or not; and I would be in a position to determine what areas there may be or what areas there will be that we're on different pages, and resolve those areas before I proceed with my cross-examination of this witness. I hope I was clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah. As I understand you saying we should proceed and later on you be given underlying source documents. I'm not sure whether they are available.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And I don't know if they're not available how then are you going to cure the problem later. I'm not quite sure. Madam Sutherland, do you have those documents?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Defence has been given all of the underlying documents to Mr. Treanor's report. In relation to what's been referred to as the CaseMap, it's not the practice of the ICTY, especially in -- well, not especially, in relation to experts that -- that sort of information is disclosed. I mean the Defence have the expert report, they have all the underlying documents that have been cited in that report. We would be opposed to that at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Except as the Chamber has rightfully pointed out. We normally are all on the same page, speaking the same language, dealing with the same information. That is not the case here. We have unique situation by virtue of the fact that the witness has a skill which he has used for purposes of preparing his report; and we don't have that information, which normally we would. And, you know, I understand that the Prosecution takes the position that it's not the -- they put it in the terms of the practice, I don't think that that's really the ultimate issue here, and I don't mean to be radical in any fashion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's not practice, maybe, because it has never been requested. If it was requested then they may have to supply it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It has been requested in the past, and it hasn't been the practice that it has been disclosed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And haven't been ordered in the past to disclose it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You might be some time in the future. Now, I think we have heard enough about the objection. We need to rule on it, now at this stage, unless anybody else has anything to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can I just add, Your Honour, in case I wasn't clear before; the Defence has made this blanket objection in relation to draft translations in relation to documents used by Mr. Treanor, given what I said before about the -- you know, the Bench has to make a balance, they have to strike a balance between the fairness to the accused and -- and considerations of judicial economy related to the organisation of the ICTY and the translation services. The additional work that would be borne by the translation services would be considerable, if we were to get --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You made that point yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: But unless --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me correct you, there was not a blanket objection. There was an objection to a specific document that was on the screen yesterday in both B/C/S and English; and this witness said he is looking at the B/C/S, works straight from the B/C/S, this translation. He doesn't look at, and it is a translation that is not by CLSS; and these translations can have inaccuracies at some times. So there was a specific objection to a specific document. Now -- and I think have I heard what you said about judicial economy and the resources of CLSS. You made that point yesterday and the Bench is mindful of what you said. It has not forgotten. So I ask you to please not repeat yourself.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may just take you to page 942 the Defence said, when I specifically asked whether they were in fact making an objection whether they had an objection to the draft translations, and Mr. Guy-Smith said: "With regard to those documents that Mr. Treanor is using which are draft translations, in the absence of information at the present time concerning the accuracy of those translations, we object."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker please be asked to slow down. It is impossible to follow at this pace, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're asked to slow down. Can you repeat yourself, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: At page 942, and this was in relation to a specific question to the Defence as to whether they objected to all the documents, and Mr. Guy-Smith said at line 13: "With regard to those documents that Mr. Treanor is using which are draft translations, in the absence of information at the present time concerning the accuracy of those translations we object."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I might, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You pointed out specifically why this whole issue arose because of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Also don't repeat what has already been said to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No. Because of the comments made on page 929. But if we continue looking at what I said with regard to this specific issue, I was quite particularised, as a result of the experience that he had just had, in terms of the specific document that you yourself were discussing with Ms. Sutherland which I raised earlier on -- so it's -- it's an inaccurate presentation presently made by the Prosecution, and the omission --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Bench is aware of that. I think we've got to rule, and ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm afraid the ruling is going to be somewhat extended, and it's going to go like this. Your objection is upheld, Mr. Guy-Smith, and in resolving the matter on the way forward, the Trial Chamber gives the following ruling: Mr. Treanor, you will be allowed to carry on testifying. You shall use in your testifying the English version, English translations, and not the B/C/S version. The Prosecution shall make sure that as soon as possible provides official translations of all the quotations that need to be translated, and at that stage the Defence will make up its mind whether, based on the official translations and the mistakes that may have been pointed out by Mr. Treanor, whether this is an need to recall him or to raise any issue with the Bench.
