utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yesterday we had -- they put them on the e-court thing. They had the English and the -- you will look at the English so that we all are looking at the same.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could perhaps suggest a slight variation of that -- no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The order has been made. Sorry, you can't. Yes, Madam Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, is it possible in the break that the Prosecution can provide Mr. Treanor with a copy of the English translations so that at least he has them in front of him as opposed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Whatever you please. So long as whatever you give him is the same as what you are going to mount on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We've got five minutes to break.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the registrar call up Rule 65 ter number 06739, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And page 10 in the B/C/S and page 11 in the e-court and the B/C/S is obviously for the benefit of the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is not, ma'am. Except for picking up any discrepancies on the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor my question to you yesterday was did the idea of assisting Serbs outside of Serbia find any additional expression at that time, and you started to testify about this document. If you can begin where we left or in fact summarise what you said yesterday and then move on.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, just to recall, this is the programme of the socialist party of Serbia adopted at its founding congress on 16th of July 1990. I wanted to call the Trial Chamber's attention to the first paragraph under the heading which, in the English says, "Serbian diaspora." I was going to provide my own translation of that from Serbian. I… and now we can all look at the English and we are all working from the English, I will have to have a look at that and just note the fact that it speaks about providing assistance to portions of the Serbian people living in other republics and recall in this connection that the new socialist party of Serbia was in fact the ruling party in Serbia at that time, they were in a position to give effect to their programme since they were in power. I would also call the Trial Chamber's attention to the fifth paragraph under the heading, "National equality, federalism," where they make reference to a new Yugoslav constitution and the formation of autonomous provinces in Yugoslavia. The Yugoslav constitution would have been the constitution that might have been produced out of the discussions that were going on about the reform of the Yugoslav system, and the programme is advocating the formation of autonomous provinces. As part of that constitution, under the old constitutions there were only autonomous provinces within Serbia. There were no autonomous provinces in the other republics. So what is in effect being suggested here is that perhaps autonomous provinces could be formed in other republics as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And did that idea remain the same in 1991?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as we will see in further documents, Serbian autonomous provinces were in fact formed within Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, which I will refer to as BH. They were formed by the local Serbian authorities in those republics.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, just as a matter in relation to MFIing these documents, I omitted yesterday in relation to the two that were shown to the witness, to ask for them to be MFIed at that point. Should we do this now, before the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... which were shown to the witness yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Rule 65 number 06812, and this document we're talking about is now which is 06739.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 06812 was not even admitted just yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No. That's what I'm saying, Your Honour. I wish to mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And I will actually give you the page of the transcript that it was referred to so that we're not ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 65 ter 06812 from yesterday is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number and marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may that document was first called up at page 925 of the transcript yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 06812 will be Exhibit P150, marked for identification Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The next one is 06739.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And if I may, Your Honour, that was called up at page 931.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P151, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Would then be this -- would this then be a convenient time, Madam Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll take a break and come back at 4.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you proceed, Madam Sutherland, let me just clarify the ruling that the Chamber gave. I just didn't sort of -- didn't occur to me when you asked that -- that 65 ter 06812 be MFIed. I don't think there's a need to MFI it because it was not objected against. We MFI 06739, that is the only one that, at this point, the Chamber is ordering the Prosecution to give official translation. However, as regards the witness, right through his testimony, he must read the English. Okay?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So anything else will have to be objected to before an order can be given and what should be done with it, everything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Just so I make sure I'm clear on the rulings of the road. With regard to any further exhibits that are used by the witness in the event there is an objection, I should make it at that time so that the record is clear if that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay, very good. I have a quick question based upon the Chamber's previous ruling, which is, I don't know whether or not the witness is in possession of any notes independent of his report for purposes of assisting him in his testimony; and I would just like to be clear about the fact is what is the document or the binder that he have in front of him at this point so, once again, we're all working on the same page. I don't have if very any special notes that exist independent of the document itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sure can you find that out during your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Would the registrar call up Rule 65 ter number 06628.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. Madam Registrar, will you please delete MFI to yesterday's -- 65 ter 6812. It will be an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will now be Exhibit P150, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You were calling?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, this is a speech to the presidents of the municipalities of the Republic of Serbia by Slobodan Milosevic. Can you tell the Court the significance of Mr. Milosevic's speech on the 16th of March, 1991, if can you confirm that date.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the date of the speech. I'd just like to provide a little bit of context first for the speech which takes place several months later than the last document we saw. In the intervening period, the new constitution of Serbia had been adopted on the 28th of September 1990; on the same date it was announced that multi-party elections would take place in December. They took place in December. They were elections for the new national assembly of Serbia and for the new office of president of Serbia, previously there had been only been a Presidency with a president of the Presidency. Slobodan Milosevic was elected president of Serbia by a substantial majority, I think about 65 per cent. His party the SPS the Socialist Party of Serbia did not win a majority of the votes in the election. However, they did win a large majority of the seats in the assembly so they were still the ruling party. In March, the time -- the month that the speech was given, there were demonstrations in Belgrade, beginning on the 9th of March in -- protesting against the control of the press. There were counter-demonstrations. The army appeared in the streets for a while. This speech was delivered in the midst of that series of demonstrations, and in the portions that we're going to be looking at here, Slobodan Milosevic refers to some of the points that we have seen already in relation to the future of Yugoslavia rather than the internal situation in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If the registrar can highlight the text starting with the sentences: "We told them ... gentlemen" on page 1 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Highlight ...

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Blow up, Your Honour. I have been told it's already at its maximum.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So, Dr. Treanor, please take the Trial Chamber to the portions that you deem important.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, in the sentence beginning on the fifth line from the top, we told them, gentleman, I'd like to call the Court' attention to that passage. The gentlemen being referred to are Croatian leaders or at least Croatian officials. He is referring to discussions that they have been having, the Serbian leader have been having with Croatian leaders about the future of Yugoslavia during this period beginning in February 1991. It continued for several months. There were periodic meetings among the presidents of all the republics to Yugoslavia to resolve the issue of the future of the country and the two main options that were -- figured in those discussions were confederation versus federation. Two concepts we have already seen. Here Milosevic is expressing his -- the basis for his -- part of the basis for his objection to the idea of a confederation; namely, that it would make Serbs living outside of Serbia national minorities in independent states.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could go to page two.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd now like to call the Court's attention to the -- I think it's the third full paragraph on that page, beginning with: "We must ensure unity in Serbia." And here Mr. Milosevic again refers to the idea of borders which he describes as an essential state issue and expresses the thought that borders are always decided by the strong.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we can go to page 3. Page 3 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we saw before, he had indicated in one of the -- I think the first speech we saw, that if it was -- if a confederation was to come about that the question of the borders would be reopened. Now, on page 3 right at the very top, I'd just like to point out that in the first two lines, he indicates that he has been in touch with Serbian leaders in Croatia and Bosnia, Knin being the centre of the Croatian Serbs. And the paragraph goes on to describe the situation as Milan Babic, the leader of the Croatian Serbs, has related to him. Then toward the bottom of that paragraph, I would call the Court's attention to the second-to-last sentence, beginning with: "I hope that we shall not have these problems." Here he refers to one of the solutions that he favours for solving the impasse over the future of the country; namely the idea of a referendum of nations. He made a distinction, a sharp distinction between a referendum within a given republic, as opposed to a referendum among members a particular nation; for instance, the Serbian nation. He was not willing to accept, for instance, that a referendum would be held in Croatia and the majority of people in Croatia would vote for the independence of Croatia for instance by outvoting the Serbs in Croatia. He was perfectly happy to see the Croats leave Yugoslavia, if they so desired, but that nations that wanted to stay within Yugoslavia - for instance the Serbs - should be permitted to do so, and the method he proposed to accomplish that by was by referendum -- a referendum among individual nations in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What was Mr. Milosevic's position --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, if I might, I'm sorry, and I understand that the witness has been asked to point out areas that he believed are important but there -- no question has been directed with regard to what the importance is of these areas. He then has recited a particular passage and then from then has included information that may well be within the context of this particular speech or passage, or may not be. But right now, the question and answer procedures is relatively free flowing. What is of importance to the witness, among other things is most probably irrelevant unless this is a question directed as to why he is giving these particular response, which we don't have any guidance for right now. And I suggest that we have a question devoted to the witness other than what is the next thing you believe to be of importance, because that is irrelevant, what he believes to be important, in the context of the manner of the questioning thus far. It is not connected to a subject. It's connected to an internal thinking process which we have not been exposed to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Treanor gave evidence about the formation of the autonomous provinces of Yugoslavia, and then I asked him about this next document to -- did that idea remain the same and brought this document up. He was explaining how Milosevic addressed a number of persons and told them basically we will ensure unity in Serbia. He is answering my questions and doing it through a document and directing to Your Honours to what he deems is to be the most important paragraphs in those documents. He can simply direct Your Honours to those paragraphs but give you his evidence in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The nub of the objection is that you -- excuse me, I'm sorry. You as the person asking questions should put a question to him that demonstrates why that portion that he is dealing with should be regarded as important, not just say and then page 3 of English and then he looks at the paragraph, talks and then page 4. That's the point of the objection. Not that you are not asking question but that are you not asking a question that should illustrate why that particular passage is being chosen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm going to object to another problem. I notice that the witness is reading his binder in Serbian as opposed to confining himself to dealing with the English translations. So he is apparently preparing himself for something, I don't know the exact nature of which, which is outside of the purview which the questioning process was to occur.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it correct, Mr. Treanor, that you're looking at your Serbian documents there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed I'm under the impression that have I been invited to call the Court's attention to any discrepancies that I see between Serbian and English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure. Indeed you have been. You have looked at the Serbian documents; you know what the Serbian documents say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I don't have them memorized though and I have just been given the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then it -- okay. To that extent, you are allowed to look at them. If can you sort of demonstrate the significance of the passages that you are -- he is being directed to.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, the significance -- I mean, I don't want to give evidence from the bar table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] MS. SUTHERLAND.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So, Mr. Treanor, what was the significance of ensuring unity in Serbia and the issue of the borders?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Milosevic indicates that Serbia had to be strong in order to obtain the borders that it might desire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That is not an answer to the question, Mr. Treanor. You're repeating what Milosevic is saying. The question is what is the significance of what -- of wanting to be strong, to obtain their desires.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it -- I could indicate, as is indicated in the next passage that I'd like to direct the Court's attention to, in the same document, which is on page 4 of the English. Toward the bottom of the page, just above where it says, "Cvetkovic," out in the left hand -- Mr. Milosevic indicates that if anyone wanted to secede from Yugoslavia by attacking Serbian settlements that the -- that the army might intervene. In other words, the use of force and a show of strength might be necessary to prevent attacks on Serbian settlements and the purpose of which will be presumably to take them out of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What was Mr. Milosevic's position, after Slovenia and Croatia declared independence at the end of June 1991?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the next document that we're going to look at will indicate that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If 65 ter number 06667 could be shown, please. Sorry, can I -- can I tender that document into evidence, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We would object to the admission of this document at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mm-hm. Basis?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I have noted that there are some differences between information that is contained in Mr. Treanor's report, in terms of translation and the document itself. And in the absence of being able to go through this document completely, and specifically with regard to those portions just testified to by Mr. Treanor, in terms of the accuracy of the information contained therein, we would object. Because I can't -- my concern is that if Mr. Treanor is indicating at this point that he does not have any distinction as between his -- his interpretation/translation of the document, that was in English and this is not an official translated document, we're in a position where we can't agree at the moment to this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Guy-Smith. What is the discrepancy? We're in the dark. You picked up the discrepancy between the information in the report and the translations. What is that discrepancy?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It is on -- in his report -- I'm sorry. Just a minute, please. In his report, which is 65 ter number 06646-01, with regard to the specific issue of strength, as he is characterizes it, he indicates in his report at page 11 that, at the very bottom of the page, with regard to what he has quoted, the last two sentences: "These are issues of the borders; therefore, essential state issues and borders, as you know, are always dictated by the strong, never by the weak." And the term "dictated" as opposed to the term "decided" have a context just difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where is decided mentioned? Here it says dictated where you referred us to and where is decided mentioned not with the previous page on this document, on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I believe it would be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we go back to the previous page, please. In the English, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I can assist, Your Honour, it's on page 2, at the middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mm-hm. It hasn't been tendered yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, at page 2 in the middle of the page, it says: "The border should, therefore, is an essential state issue and as you know borders are always decided upon by the strong, never the weak."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm just waiting for the page to be turned.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: While we're waiting, your learned friend conceded that it says decided there, I guess you are, Madam Sutherland. Does the document on the screen talk of decided, do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The document says decided, yes; and the report says dictated.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well. I withdraw my objection, and then I guess I withdraw my objection at this time and aware that it is a matter of the accuracy of the report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well I think I get to say something.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Treanor there is it no pending question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Treanor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure. Sorry, sorry. Mr. Treanor, as I indicated to you earlier, when this is an objection you're out of it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. So you withdraw your objection. You may proceed, Madam Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So, Your Honours, that is admitted into evidence, that document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. It will have to be MFIed because your learned friend has now raised an objection, at least there is a difference that you agree that the one document says "decided" the other one says "dictated." This is it, 06628, isn't it? Is that it?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay, fine.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P152, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the registrar please call up Rule 65 ter 06667.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, you asked for this document to be called up in relation to the question that I put to you.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I be allowed to comment on discrepancy between the translation -- that you have been provided and my rendering of the previous document, an issue which has been broached?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You can offer the discrepancies, explanation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry I didn't earlier, Your Honour. I have just been presented with these documents in English which I have never seen them before, and I'm new to this particular process. In the Serbian, the word that apparently rendered as decided or decide in the translation is "dikteriu," [phoen] which is a much stronger term which I rendered as dictated or dictate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will wait for official translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour. I do note in the English translation that the sentence starts: "We must ensure unity in Serbia if we want to dictate the course of the events."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure. But that is it not the sentence that was being referred to by Mr. Guy-Smith. It's a different sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's the same verb used later on in that passage. So the same verb has been translated in different ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think that's why we have the benefit of CLSS so they can make an independent determination of what is accurate or appropriate unless at this time Mr. Treanor is offering himself also as an expert, as a translator, which I don't think he was proffered as.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I note for the record that is a final CLSS translation that we're looking at on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's fine. We've got to resolve the problems. The point of the matter it may very well, Mr. Treanor, that we still need the official translation from CLSS. We note your pointing the difference and talking about it, and giving your view about it; but, still, we must await the official translation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, if you can proceed to answer the question that was put to you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could you repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It was, what was Mr. Milosevic's position after Slovenia and Croatia declared their independence at the end of June 1991.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that connection, I would direct the Court's attention to the last paragraph on this page. The sentence beginning with: "Serbia's standpoint is that all disputes can be solved peacefully." And he advocates that the solution be based on respect or the right to self-determination of peoples. And if we can move to the next page. And then he concludes that the passage by saying: "The Yugoslav People's Army should provide the aforementioned peoples with support and with the support of all the political institutions and peace forces." So he is suggesting that the Yugoslav People's Army can be -- can play a role in that process.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What was happening on the ground at this time?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pardon me, I think we lost track of the course of the developments. I think you mentioned that Croatia and Slovenia had declared independence on the 25th of June, 1991. The speech was delivered a week or so later. Fighting had broken out in Slovenia and by this time had stopped, but the situation in Croatia was becoming very tense.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I would ask for that document to be admitted, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 65 ter 06667 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P153, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, if we can start with the Serbs in the Republic of Croatia. What were their basic principles and goals?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we're moving on to the next document now?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could I have Rule 65 ter number --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or we haven't quite finished with this one. I think there may be ... I wanted to call the Court's attention to the second sentence in the next paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry which document are we dealing with?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry we're back on 06667, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure. They have been --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry P153, I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Make sure you are conducting the proceedings, ma'am. Okay, what page is that? Same page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the page that is on the screen, Your Honour, in the next paragraph, he makes reference to the -- his belief that the Yugoslav People's Army should be present in the territories inhabited by the peoples that have chosen to live in Yugoslavia. He gets more specific about what he thinks the role of the army should be in this situation, among the peoples, of course, that ones that remained in Yugoslavia was the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, can we, looking at document, Rule 65 ter number 06702, what were the basic principle and goals for the Serbian people in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. Now we're moving back a little bit in time to follow developments on a little bit closer to the ground in Croatia, specifically among the Serbs in Croatia. I mentioned before that in 1990 the process had begun of the formation of non-Communist political parties in the various republics in Yugoslavia. The particular document in front of us now is a founding document of what was known as the Serbian Democratic Party in Croatia and among other things this document sets out its programmatic goals; and I just want to draw the Court's attention to one point in that programme.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I think if the registrar can bring up page number 15 of the English translation and it's page number 9 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here we see the newly formed party advocating the idea of the formation of what refers to as territorial autonomies within Yugoslavia. Again, reference is made to federalism; that is, territorial autonomies within a federal Yugoslavia. The term, "territorial autonomies" was one that was later used in the new constitution of the Republic of Serbia referred to earlier. It used that phrase to describe type of autonomy that that constitution provided for the provinces of Vojvodina and Kosovo. So, here, the Serbian Democratic Party in Croatia is advocating that type of solution as well and would like to see that happen in Croatia on the basis of a referendum.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask that that document be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be Exhibit P154, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor was this territorial autonomy realized in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at this time. The document we just saw, February 1990, was issued before the elections in Croatia, the multi-party elections which took place in April, which resulted in the victory of the Croatian democratic community, the HDZ, which was a non-Communist party led by Franjo Tudjman. That party formed the government, the new government of the Croatia; and Franjo Tudjman was elected president of the Presidency of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were any --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That government was not disposed to -- to grant territorial autonomy to -- at that time to the Serbs in Croatia, and in fact proceeded with the process of drafting a new constitution for Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Just briefly, were there any community of municipalities constituted in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On their own initiative, certain municipalities in Croatia, which -- which had Serbian majorities, formed after the elections in Croatia, what they called a community of municipalities. That was at the end of June 1990. The -- within the Yugoslav system, communities of municipalities were a recognised substitution they were ordinarily formed by municipalities in a republic that had similar interests; for instance developing the tourist trade and they would band together for the purpose of promoting the joint interests in that area. They were voluntary associations. They didn't have any power to make laws. They -- they could, however, agree among themselves as to certain courses of action which the municipal assemblies would have to adopt. The one that was formed in Croatia that we're referring to by the Serbian municipalities did not in fact really assign itself any particular function.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, may that -- no, that is already admitted, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, what further steps did the Serbs in Croatia take in pursuit of the goals? Was any declaration made by them?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think the next document we'll see --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If 65 ter 06709 could be brought up.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document provides a little more concrete expression as to what certain Serbian leaders in Croatia striving for at this time. This document is dated the 25th of July, 1990, about a month after the community of municipalities was formed. This is a declaration that was adopted at a meeting of what was called a Serbian Assembly in the village of Srb in Croatia on that date, and this declaration asserts that the Serbian people in Croatia are a sovereign people. That's in the -- item number 1. And then in the next paragraph, it -- the next paragraph on the page we were looking at. It asserts that the Serbian nation in Croatia is entitled to opt either for a federal or a confederal system, a state, either jointly with the Croatian nation or independently. So it is raising the idea here that the Serbian nation in Croatia could become independent of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did they take steps to do that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as part of this particular document, if we can go to item number 3 on the next page. Must be the next page in the English. This declaration establishes a -- what is called as a -- the Serbian Assembly as the political representative of the Serbian people. So they began to establish their own hierarchical structure. And as an executive organ for that assembly, it established a -- which is here referred to as a Sabor, it established as a executive organ a Serbian National Council in -- which is further described in paragraph number 4 on that page, referring to a referendum of the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, may that document be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P155, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, was the referendum, in fact, held?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The -- I think the next document will tell us something about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Rule 65 ter number 06704, please. Page 2 of the English translation and page 1 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What document is this, Dr. Treanor -- Mr. Treanor.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: We see here a report on the results of the referendum. The report states that the Serbian National Council, in fact, decided to hold a referendum of the Serbian people in Croatia, a decision that was taken on the 16th of August, 1990. And the report indicates that voting was, in fact, carried out; and the results are given in paragraph 3. Or it gives the number of people who voted in favour of Serbian autonomy, which is the overwhelming majority of people that, according to the report, participated in this referendum. So here we have the -- a declaration, an assertion, a confirmation of the desire of the Serbian people in Croatia for autonomy.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, can that document be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P156, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: After the referendum, did the Serbs in Croatia further develop the use of Serbian autonomy and, in fact, institute it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can we have Rule 65 ter number 06436.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, you said, Yes. When did this occur?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this document is dated the 19th of December, 1990. This was just a few days before the proclamation of the new constitution of Croatian, an event which took place on the 22nd of December, 1990. Many Serbs in Croatia were dissatisfied with that new constitution. It did not provide for a type of autonomous region that they might have wanted, and it failed to mention the Serbian people in the constitution as one of the constituent nations of Croatia. We see in this document -- the proclamation -- or the statute of a so-called Serbian Autonomous District or region. I'm not sure which translation is being given here. Because I don't see the first page. But I would just like to call the Court's attention to Article 1 which is being displayed. Yes, it says here the Serbian Autonomous District of Krajina will be a form of territorial autonomy within Croatia. Again, the use of the expression, "territorial autonomy." If I could just check that in the original, which I think I can read on the screen. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, may that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Article further states the purpose for the establishment of the Serbian Autonomous District, which is namely to safeguard the -- among other things the national equality of the Serbian people in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, may that document be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P157, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, did the SAO Krajina disassociate itself from the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think we're going to see a document on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: May I have Rule 65 ter number 06699. Page 2 of the English translation and page 1 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is a resolution adopted by the Serbian National Council on the 28th of February, 1991. This resolution was adopted, I believe, two days after the Assembly of the Republic of Croatia adopted a resolution which, foresaw a negotiating process or participating in a negotiating process for the breakup of the former Yugoslavia and foresaw the establishments of the republics as independent states and expressed a willingness to enter into various types of association with the other republics on the basis of the independence of each of them. This was precisely what many of the Serbs in Croatia did not want to see happen. So we see in this resolution, in the first paragraph, its rejection -- the Serbian National Council of the idea of separating from Yugoslavia; and in the paragraph 4, which I would call the Court's attention, the resolution states that federal laws and the laws of the Serbian Autonomous District would be applied in the territory of the Serbian Autonomous District and the laws of Croatia would only be applied if they were not in opposition to those laws. So this represents a major step towards separating from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, may that document be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P158, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You mentioned that it represented a major step towards separating from Croatia. Was a decision ever made to join the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We'll see -- the next document relating to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Rule 65 number 06740, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When was this?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document represents a decision passed by the Executive Council of the Serbian Autonomous District of Krajina on the 1st of April, 1991. This was, I think, six days after the Croatian Assembly passed a resolution calling for a referendum in Croatia on the issue of independence and federation. The referendum question had -- two referendum questions: one related to whether people wanted Croatia to be a sovereign and independent state, and the other question was whether they wished to remain within the Yugoslav federation. Those were to be the questions in a referendum scheduled for May. So we see this decision, passed on the 1st of April, which as we can see in Article 1 to which I draw the Court's attention, the Serbian Autonomous District is now said to join itself to the Republic of Serbia. And Article 2 goes on to describe that, stating that the laws of Serbia will now be valid in the Serbian Autonomous Districts.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the legal regulations that are in force within the SAO Krajina?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again those are said to be the laws of the Republic of Serbia and of the SFRY. That is, the Federation. Again, in Article 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Does this decision make reference to whether the SAO Krajina is going to become part of a unitary state?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it makes reference to Serbia as being a unitary state. That is, Serbia itself not being a federation or a confederation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, may that document be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P159, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What decisions were taken at the 1st Assembly of the SAO Krajina?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the next document we're going to see is a decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could Rule 65 ter number 06666.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: A decision adopted at that session on the 30th of April, 1991, which elects Milan Babic as the president of the Executive Council of the Serbian Autonomous District of Krajina. The translation uses the word "region" here which is the translation of the same word that was translated as "district" in the previous documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And in that document it is decided to hold a referendum. Is that the case? What is the question for the referendum?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This document does not mention referendum. May I skipped one? Have I skipped one. I'm sorry, yes. It's the previous document. Which is a decision made on the same day. The previous document in my binder. Perhaps it's the next one in your series. They were two decisions adopted by the Executive Council of the Serbian Autonomous Region on the 1st of April.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: First of all, if document number 06666 can be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Document 06666 the document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P160, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can we have Rule 65 ter number 06717.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, was a referendum, in fact, held? And what were the -- what was decided as to that referendum?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I mentioned that a referendum had been scheduled by the Republic of Croatia to take place on the -- it was the 19th of May. The Serbs in Croatia, pursuant to a decision by the Serbian National -- the Serbian Autonomous District held their own referendum on the 12th of May, and I would direct the Court's attention to Article 1 of this decision. Which says that on the basis of the results of that referendum the SAO Krajina, the Serbian Autonomous District of Krajina, is to remain in a joint state in Yugoslavia with Serbia, Montenegro, and others who wish to preserve Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry -- I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Perhaps I'm reading a different document than that which the witness is discussing. Article 1, as I see it, doesn't discuss any basis of any referendum. It just discusses a fact in terms of what occurred.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Perhaps I'm looking at the wrong document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Bench is looking at a document which says: "Decision on-calling a referendum on the accession of SAO Krajina to the Republic of Serbia and on remaining Yugoslavia with Serbia, Montenegro and others who want to preserve Yugoslavia." And Article 1 then says: "Referendum on the accession of SAO Krajina to the Republic of Serbia and on remaining in Yugoslavia with Serbia Montenegro and others who want to preserve Yugoslavia is hereby being called."

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Right. As I understood it Article 1 dealt with the fact of a referendum being called and nothing more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. That's what I'm looking at. Are we on the same page, Madam Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Yes, Your Honour that is what Mr. Treanor just said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't appear to have that document in my binder. That's why I was confused. I'm sorry for the confusion I caused. This is this another decision passed at that session on the 30th of April that we saw the other two decisions from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Say that again?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The document that we're looking at which is 06717, is dated the 17th of May, 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, then, I've got a problem, because Article 2 of this document says the referendum will be carried out in the territory of Serbian Autonomous Region, Krajina on the 12th of April, 1991, a date that has already passed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I'm sorry. It's my fault for the confusion. This, I assume.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And, Mr. Treanor, can you shed any light on it. Is this the date of the publication of the Official Gazette?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is does not look like something from the Official Gazette. What I'm looking at on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If you can -- the page -- the English translation be the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you referring to 17th of May, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Is the date when the Official Gazette was published, the 17th of May?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If I can see the previous page in the Serbian. If we could blow that up. I'm sorry, I don't have this document in my binder. This is a decision that was passed on the 30th of April at the session I referred to before.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And that's in the first paragraph of the English translation, is it not?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the preamble. Pursuant to the people's right. At the last line it says that a session held on 30th of April, 1991. And Article 2 does in fact say that it will be held on 12/04/91 that is the 12th of April, 1991, which is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you say the decision was on the 30th of April then the date has passed already.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is obviously a misprint.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: A typographical error in the --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, I don't think anyone at this point is qualified to discuss what that is. Whether it's obviously a misprint or anything else questions. Obviously some questions about the -- this particular document, potentially the authenticity of this document, and whether or not this document is an official document; and I don't think any conjecture should be made in the absence to further qualifications with regard to such matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, can we mark this document for identification, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It may be so marked and be given exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will Exhibit P161, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, can I just take to you Article 3?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Article 3 of what, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Of the document we were just looking at, P161.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What does Article 3 state?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Article 3 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we push up the English, please.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- relates to the question that will be used at the referendum; namely do you support the accession of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Article -- oh.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the next page in the English it has the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Page 2 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: And as the Court can see, the question is: Do you support the accession of the SAO, that is Serbian Autonomous District of Krajina to the Republic of Serbia, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were any constitutional laws proclaimed by the SAO Krajina?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After the referendum, which we have been discussing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter number 06441 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What were the constitutional laws that were proclaimed?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 29th of May, 1991, it would have within ten days after the Croatian referendum on the 19th of May a referendum which produced very large majorities in favour of a sovereign and independent Croatia and against remaining in the Yugoslavia federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I do apologise, sir. That is non-responsive to the question that was asked. The specific question was asked, which was, What were the constitutional laws that were proclaimed. If he wishes to explain something thereafter, that's a different matter, but he should be directed to answer the question posited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think in answering my question Dr. Treanor is giving the background to the -- to the law that was proclaimed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: But, Mr. Treanor, can you answer in -- in one sentence what were the constitutional laws which were proclaimed?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the -- again on the 29th of May, the Assembly of the Serbian Autonomous District of Krajina, adopted a constitutional law which we see before us, in which I would call the Court's attention to Article 1 in which reference is now made to the Serbian Autonomous District of Krajina as a form of political and territorial autonomy within federative Yugoslavia. As the Court will recall the phrase territorial autonomy had been used now that that is being expanded to describe this district as having political territorial autonomy. Further on in the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That's on page 3 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would call the Court's attention to Article 6 of this constitutional law, which establishes the -- various organs of government for the autonomous district.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: May that be admitted into evidence -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, the particular Article goes on to -- states that the Autonomous District will pass laws as opposed to the earlier community of municipalities in the earlier forms of autonomy they were claiming. They will now actually pass laws within the autonomous district.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P162, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was going to call the Court's attention to Article 9 of that decision as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Wait for questions from counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were the -- was any decision taken as to the implementation of the decisions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure I understand the question. Maybe if you understand, you can answer it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the organs referred to in the -- in the decision were in fact -- did in fact begin to function.

utterances.text: Thank you. Let take a break. We'll come back at quarter to. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor we were looking at Exhibit P162, and I was talking you -- I misspoke and said I wanted you to look at Article 9. If you could look at Article 6, subparagraph 9. Article 6, then paragraph numbered 9.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And of course my question was: Was that law that was adopted make reference to the implementation of the decisions? If could you look --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As point 9 makes mention of the -- ensuring the implementation of decisions?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And is that what you were referring to earlier?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the implementation is concerned, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can document Rule 65 ter number 066790 be brought on the screen, please. Can we go to page 50 of the English translation and page 83 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, in relation to the announcement by Milosevic that you talked about earlier in your testimony, did the JNA enforce the borders?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This document is a little more specific than the Milosevic speech that we saw published on the 7th of July in which he refers to the JNA --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And what is it --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- preserving Yugoslavia within new frameworks as he said on the basis of the right of the peoples to self-determination. I would direct the Court's attention to --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And first of all, what is this document?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This document is the verbatim record of a session of the Serbian National Assembly held, I believe, on the 26th of September, 1991. At this time the fighting in Croatia had greatly intensified compared to the situation in early July. The bottom paragraph of the page we're looking at, which is page 50 of the translation, indicates what the Speaker sees as the aim of the JNA in Croatia. The Speaker, by the way, is Borisav Jovic, who was the -- who was a member of the Presidency of the SFRY. He was the member from Serbia. So he was a important member of the Serbian leadership. He notes in the paragraph that the aim of the army in Croatia is not to topple the Croatian government but to promote the right of every nation to self-determination and particularly promoting the right of -- to protect the Serbian people in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Does this document set out what the goals of what the army are?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Even more specific is a passage further on, on page 91 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And that's on page 149 of the B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry, Madam Sutherland. Your learned friend is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, I don't know whether or not the witness misspoke himself, at line seven, the document says -- he used the word particularly promoting and dealing with particularly, and the word that is actually in the document itself is "practically" promoting. I don't know whether he misspoke himself. I just wanted to deal with that as a potential correction to the statement now. So we didn't lose sight of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What was the correct point you wanted to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: On line 7 it says particularly and the word is practically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Treanor, did you mean to say particularly or did you mean it say practically.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honour, I meant to say particularly. I wasn't reading from the English. I was trying to briefly summarize some of the words that are in the translation that we can all see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: On page 91 --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, then. If he is summarizing a part of a document, a specific phrase of a document where he uses 99.9 per cent of the words that are contained in the phrase and one would think he should remain consistent if he now wishes to render -- assuming it is of any use to the Chamber based on what his summary may be, if he wishes to render some opinion, that is a different matter; and whether or not his summary admits to an opinion as a historical matter is an entirely different question. But right now for purposes of discussion the document -- I mean -- if I'm not mistaken that the only distinction is between "practical" and "particularly," and since words can be used either as swords or shield and specifically here where the interpretation of is of some moment, if he is going to be dealing with a particular passage and highlighting it for the Chamber's attention; and I think it would be appropriate to be spot-on accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any response, Madam Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, in relation to the Defence objection, Your Honour, I think that Mr. Treanor can -- can give his opinion as to whether he thinks that the word is better particularly used or practically in that sentence. The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But did you hear the gravamen of the objection. The gravamen of the objection is that --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- every other word he is paraphrasing is exactly as it is in the document, and it is only one word that differs; and we don't know why he chooses to depart what is on the document to what he is now saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. If Mr. Treanor is going to summarize a portion of the transcript -- the document, then he needs to, if he is going to use a different word in that summarisation, then needs to justify why he is changing the word, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now he hasn't done so.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No. I'm just about to ask him whether he wants to justify why he used the words particularly as opposed to practically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that a question? I would be happy to withdraw the word particularly and replace it with practically. In the interest of being spot-on accurate, I will simply read out the entirety of all the passages that have been selected in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. It would actually be helpful if you do that, Mr. Treanor, because if you are telling us of what is written, it is important to read it exactly as it is without embellishment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very good, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, if we could go to the passage on page 91 of the translation and page 149 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just below the centre of the passage now at the bottom of the page on the screen there's a paragraph that I'd like to call the Court's attention to which is more specific in connection with the goal of the army. Namely it says: "The army has a strategic goal. I can tell you," I, still being Borisav Jovic. "I can tell you that clearly and surely the strategic goal of the army is to hold the Serbian territories in Croatia until the crisis is politically solved. It will withdraw its forces to these territories as much as it can, even before the crisis is solved."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, can that document be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P163, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: By the end of 1991, were the hostilities still prevailing in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: By the end of the year, meaning December, a cease-fire was in place as of the 24th of November, which seemed to be holding; so hostilities had wound down to a great extent. There was still some fighting going on, I think, notably perhaps in the Dubrovnik area. And progress was being made toward the adoption of what was known as the Vance Plan for Croatia, which involved the deployment of US -- sorry, UN peacekeeping forces in Croatia, in particular, in those parts of Croatia that were under the control of Serbian forces at that time. This document, therefore, speaks to the tasks of the army in the new situation. It was issued on the 10th of December.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could Rule 65 ter number 06625, please. Page 3 of both the B/C/S and the English. The paragraph that I'm interested in it under the Roman numeral II.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, is this the document that you were just referring to?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a directive signed by Veljko Kadijevic, general of the army. Veljko Kadijevic, who was the federal secretary for national defence. And we can see in that paragraph under Roman numeral II, he specifies that: "Our armed forces are entering a new period of exceptional significance for accomplishing the ultimate aim of the war: The protection of the Serbian population. A peaceful resolution of Yugoslavia crisis and the creation of conditions in which Yugoslavia may be preserved for those people that wish to live in it. Therefore, the preservation of the combat readiness of the JNA and the armed forces as a whole is still the central task of command and control and its members at all levels. Until such time as --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, I'm sorry. I have been following along quite well. We have just been double-checking our 65 ter lists, with regard to documents that were submitted and gone through the -- a number of them and don't seem to find this particular document as being one of the documents that was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just add if it might be of help. I don't see any Roman numeral II on this document and listening to what Mr. Treanor has been reading, it doesn't seem to tally with what I see on paragraph 2 of this document, under tasks.

utterances.text: On page 3 of the English translation, Your Honour.

utterances.text: On the top of the page on the English translation there is a Roman numeral II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO

utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor was in the middle of reading out that paragraph. The Defence had an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, I have that as a removed document from the list, according to our records. We'll double-check it. Let's just proceed. We'll just double-check it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The reason I'm raising is that I have a binder full of all -- I believe all of those are 65 ter exhibits that would be presented through this witness.
