Let's just proceed at this point, and if there is a problem, we'll pick it up at a later time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Carry on, Madam Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. This is certainly not one that would have –- I’ll withdraw that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, you were talking about -- I don't think you finished the paragraph that you were reading, the sentence that you were reading. I think you got halfway through the last sentence of that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll read the --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I think you got up to, "... the central task of command and control."

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll read that sentence again: "Therefore, the preservation of the combat readiness of the JNA and the armed forces as a whole is still the central task of command and control and its members at all levels until such time as a political solution to the Yugoslav crisis is found." The reference to a political solution is based on the fact that the Vance Plan that I mentioned was a -- a transitional measure to bring peace to the areas of -- to Croatia and have UN peacekeeping forces there to maintain that peace, pending the outcome of negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, may that document be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Sutherland, if I may just ask, how many pages is this document?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Five.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P164, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor what was the position of the Presidency of the SFRY in relation to the position taken by the Federal Secretariat for the National Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could 65 ter number 06791 on the screen, please. Pages 25 to 27 of the English translation and page 34 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think we can find the answer to that question in the document we're looking at. This is the verbatim record of a meeting that was held in Belgrade on the 12th of December at the Presidency of the SFRY. Present at this meeting were the four remaining members of the Presidency of the SFRY who were the members from Serbia and Montenegro, as well as some other high officials of the federation and numerous Serbian leaders from Croatia and Bosnia, including Radovan Karadzic and Milan Martic. Milan Babic was not at this meeting. The object of the meeting was to inform the -- what was for the federal officials to inform the Serbian leaders in Croatia and Bosnia about the Vance Plan and basically urge that they accept it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, the question put to you was: What was the position of the Presidency of the SFRY in relation to the position taken by the Federal Secretariat of National Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think we're --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you zoom in on that question and give the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think we're on page 145 of the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm advised, sir, that the document that is on the screen has only 96 pages, not 145. But in any case the question was not related to a page. The question was: What was the relation, the position of the Presidency of the SFRY in relation to the position taken by the Federal Secretariat of National Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did Mr. Milosevic have a position, does he take a position in this -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Sorry. You were asked a question earlier, we need an answer to that question. I'm trying to get an answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Will you please answer the question that was put by counsel. Do you want me it repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The question is: What was the position of the Presidency of the SFRY in relation to the position taken by the Federal Secretariat of National Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if reference is being made to the previous order, the SFRY Presidency was the Commander-in-Chief of the armed forces. So the order would have been issued under its authority.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did they --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. So you're talking in relation to a previous order? Can you talk about the Presidency of the SFRY and the Federal Secretariat of National Defence and tell us what the position of these two were in relation to each other. That's the question put to you, whatever the purpose of the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The relationship between the Presidency and the Federal Secretariat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What was the position of each in relation to each other.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Presidency of the SFRY was the Commander-in-Chief of the armed forces. The Federal Secretary of defence who signed the order that we were just looking at is the next in the chain of command in the SFRY system. So he reports as the chief military officer to the Presidency of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The question is not Secretary of Federal Secretary. It is Federal Secretariat of National Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Federal Secretariat was the bureaucratic institution that the federal secretary headed. It included the civilian components of -- included civilian components as well as the JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what was its function?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the main defence organisation -- one of the defence organisations within the SFRY. The SFRY also had a system of Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did it go by any other name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Federal Secretariat?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At this time it was still known as the Federal Secretariat for national defence. Later on under the FRY, the name would have changed to being a ministry. And each, if I can clarify, what we would, perhaps, ministries in the SFRY were called Secretariats, and the heads of those organisations were called Secretaries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, the directive that Kadijevic gave on 10th of December, 1991, said that the ultimate aim was for the protection of the Serbian population and the peaceful resolution of the Yugoslav crisis and the creation of the conditions in which Yugoslavia may be preserved. Did the Presidency of the SFRY agree with that position that was taken by the Federal Secretary of National Defence or not?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, the Presidency was the commander of the Federal Secretary, if I can put it that way and the Presidency strongly supported the self-determination certainly of the peoples including the Serbian people in Croatia and Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And so what did they have to say about it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: About this order?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What did they discuss at the meeting on the 9th of December, 1991, if you can briefly tell the Court about that.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I think I said before, this meeting was held to inform the Serbian leaders from Croatia and Bosnia who were present about the Vance Plan, which was designed to bring peace to Croatia and to urge those leaders to support it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Was there any further developments in the Croatia Krajina in -- at the end of 1991?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later in the month, the -- Serbian Autonomous District of Krajina proclaimed itself as the Republic of Serbian Krajina, in unity with two other Serbian Autonomous Districts that had been established in Croatia. That is the three Autonomous Districts joined together to form the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could I have Rule 65 ter number 06657 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What do we do with 06791?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could we admit that into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's so admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P165, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could, first of all go to pages 2 and 3 of the English translation and page 1 of the B/C/S. That's 65 ter number 06657.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, you mentioned that the SAO Krajina became the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Is the document that we're looking at the moment the constitution -- yes. What's the important provisions in this constitution that you would like to draw the Court's attention to?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would draw the Court's attention to the first two Articles, which are very brief. Article 1 stating that the Republic of Serbian Krajina shall be a national state of the Serbian people and a state of all people who live there. Article 2 goes on to state that the sovereignty shall belong to the Serbia people of the Republic of Serbian Krajina and all the citizens who live there. Serbian people and citizens of the Republic of Serbian Krajina shall realize their sovereignty through referendums national initiate and through their freely appointed representatives. I would point out that Article 1 we have the Autonomous Region under this new constitutional describing itself as -- now as a state. And it -- Article 2, I'm sorry I missed that over in the next page in the English, describes the territory of this new state which is the territory of the three Autonomous Districts as I mentioned, of the Autonomous District of Krajina. The other two Autonomous District, subsequently and indeed, one of them on the same day adopted the same constitution to effectively unite three of them in one republic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you say that is in Article 2.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Article 3, Your Honour. The territory of the Serbian Krajina shall be the territory of the Serbian Autonomous Districts of Krajina. The other two autonomous districts, Serbian Autonomous Districts in Croatia adopted the same constitution, one of them on the same day and one a few days later; and they effectively united into one republic in February of the following -- of 1992, they amended the constitution to reflect that fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And did the constitution -- sorry. Did the Republic of Serbian Krajina have its own army?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think we want to look at Article 9.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could go to page 23 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No we don't. It's Article 78. I'm sorry, we're much further along in the document, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And page 11 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And in particular, subparagraph 5 of Article 78.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This Article specifies the powers of the president of the republic, and we can see in point 5 that one of them, one of his responsibilities to is a lead the armed forces in peacetime and war time and the people's resistance in wartime, orders general and partial mobilisation and organises preparations for defence in accordance with the law. Under point 6 when the assembly is not able to meet, he detects the existence of an immediate threat of war or announces the state of war according to the Prime Minister's opinion. And under point 7 under his initiative or under the government's proposal during a state of war, or imminent threat of war adopts acts about issues from the assembly's jurisdiction and is required to submit them before the assembly as soon as the assembly is able to meet. These are some of the powers of the president under the constitution, and it's reference to the armed forces indicates that this Republic was to have its own armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did the Republic of Serbian Krajina seek recognition -- I'm sorry, Your Honour. If that document can be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P166, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could I have Rule 65 ter number 06617, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, my question was did the Republic of Serbian Krajina seek recognition?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the same day, I believe, that the constitution which we just looked at was adopted. Milan Babic, who was the president -- he was now the president of the Republic sent a letter to the European Community as we can see. It is a request for the recognition of the Republic of Serbian Krajina in the last paragraph of the letter he indicates that your conditions, meaning the European Community's conditions for the recognition are completely fulfilled by the Republic of Serbian Krajina. The reference there is to a document that the European Community had adopted, I believe, on the 16th of December which laid out certain conditions under which the European Community would recognise the independence of the republics, the individual republics of Yugoslavia should they so desire and should they so request. He here is saying that he believes we fulfil those conditions and asking for recognition as a state that is certainly independent of Croatia and apparently independent of Yugoslavia. One of the points that had to be dealt with in getting the Vance Plan accepted by the Serbian leaders in Croatia related to the fact that many of them, including Milan Babic, were very dissatisfied that that plan described their territories as being part of Croatia, whereas, as we've seen, they considered themselves to be part of Serbia and part of Yugoslavia; and they wanted to so remain. This was their response, if I can put it in that fashion, to that situation. They're declaring to the world that they're an independent state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just be clear, are you saying this document also requests recognition for the independence of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they had hitherto consider themselves to be part of Yugoslavia and Serbia in the documents that we have seen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we just look at lines 12 to 14 on page 72. On the screen and just tell -- are you mistranscribed there? You can read, independent at both places as independence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Lines 14 through --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Lines 12 through 14. He here is saying that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Yes, he is saying in effect having declared independence or having defined themselves in their constitution as a state and now asking for international recognition, they are saying that they are independent of both Croatia and Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Certainly independent of Croatia and apparently -- okay. Sorry. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, may this document be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is so admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P167, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, was a convention held in Belgrade in early 1992, in relation to territories whose population had expressed a wish to remain in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was. I think we've seen numerous references in the documents we have been looked at, to that expression, people who wished to live in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If could I have Rule 65 ter number 06681 [Realtime transcript read in error, "06682"].

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the beginning of January 1992, a big meeting described as the convention for Yugoslavia was held in Belgrade was attended by representatives from various republics mostly from Serbia and Montenegro and Serbian representatives from Bosnia and Croatia as well as a few non-Serbs who wished to continue living in Yugoslavia. They devised a plan, if you will, for the formation of a new Yugoslavia, a third Yugoslavia, which would precisely include those areas inhabited by peoples, by peoples that wished to remain living in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Who organised this conference or convention?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. Madam Sutherland did I hear you well that you asked for 65 ter 06681.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We've got 82 on the screen. Okay, it's 81. Now we know. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could just ask for pages 4 to 5 of the English translation and 4 to 5 and then later page 7 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, who organised this conference, convention?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the convention was organised under the auspices of the federal officials in Belgrade -- for instance a meeting was held in Belgrade at the Presidency at the end of December 1991, attended by many of the same people that attended the previous meeting we were looking at, Serbian -- in addition there were also some other leaders there from -- from Bosnia, and they discussed holding this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Where was the convention held?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was held at Belgrade. I can't remember which -- which building it was held in offhand. I believe it was the Sava Centre in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I can direct you to page 10 -- sorry, page 4. Did they discuss at this conference who -- who was going to -- what territory was going to form this new Yugoslavia or the new federal state?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I indicated it was to include areas inhabited by those peoples that wished to remain living in Yugoslavia. In this paragraph which comes from an article about that meeting, we see those territories specified. The magazine that this article appeared in is called the Polka [phoen], and it was connected with the socialist party of Serbia, that is Slobodan Milosevic's party. And in this paragraph we can see that it says: "The process of building new Yugoslavia will definitely depend on the will of nations, citizens, and republics that want to join it. So far, Serbia and Montenegro, Republic of Serbian Krajina and Serbian Republic of BH ... that includes Autonomous Regions of Krajina, SAO North Bosnia, SAO Semberija, SAO Romanija, and SAO Eastern Bosnia-Herzegovina, declared one way or another that they want to stay in this new federal state. All together 12 million citizens." As you can see, reference is made also to Serbian Autonomous District in Bosnia. I believe we will be seeing some documents later that relate to the development of those districts. The article is accompanied by a map, which I'm not sure how well it comes out in the black and white copies you have; but it depicts on the map the -- some territorial limits of those various Serbian Autonomous Districts.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can I direct your attention to page 5.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're seeing the map now on the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And page -- was there a debate about whether the territory should be put under the protectorate of the UN?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the reference in the article here is to the issue I referred to before. That is, the dissatisfaction in some circles with the Vance Plan. Here they -- the idea is emphasised that this is only going to be a transitional arrangement. Namely, it says: "All debatable territories should be put under the protectorate of the OUN and UN blue helmets. In this way, better protection may be provided for Serbian people in Croatia against the aggression of the Croatian army, and at the same time create the possibility for the population to declare about their new state in five or more years. In 90 per cent of the cases, the territories that had been under UN protection sooner or later got the right for independence."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, can that document be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P168, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, you mentioned that Mr. Babic, Milan Babic was the first president of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. Who was the second?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And, sorry, if can we could have Rule 65 ter number 06718 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milan Babic was replaced as president in February 1992. He had been very public in his opposition to the Vance Plan. Another big meeting was held in Belgrade beginning, I believe, on the 31st of January attended by many of the same leaders that attended the meeting in December that we were looking at. I do not have a record of that meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, may I sound a caution here. We don't have much time. There are certain questions which really don't need any background information, like the question that was asked you of you, which in fact you have not answered. You have answered it in one, two, three, four, five, six lines and two words mentioning the first name and second name of the successor will have sufficed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was just trying to explain the reasons for his removal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You were not asked about the reasons. Listen to the question, answer the question directed. If the lawyer wants reasons, she will ask you for reasons. We really don't have much time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could we go to page 4 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Have you got the answer to your question, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I just want to direct the registry so they can bring the document up while I ask the question again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Get the answer to the question because you want to make a note of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court who became president after Babic?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the 26th of February 1992 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Who.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Goran Hadzic was elected the president of the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When did this occur?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 26th of February, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the document you see on the screen is the decision taken by the Republic of Serbian Krajina assembly?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes that's the decision electing him president.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, may that be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 06718 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P169, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, who took over the Presidency from Goran Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milan Martic was the next president of the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can we have Rule 65 ter number 06788 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When did this occur?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: This occurred in January 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And what was the reason why Martic took over from Hadzic, if you know?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: They actually held elections at this time. We've seen the previous decision Goran Hadzic was elected by the assembly, but they actually held popular elections in 1994. And this document gives the results of the elections.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, may that be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's so admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P170, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You mentioned that the Republic of Serbian Krajina had an armed force. What was the name of that army?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was known as -- or at least a certain point in time became known as the Serbian army of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the acronym for that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's SVK in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: After Martic became president on the 25th of January, or in January 1994 who was appointed as military commander of the SVK?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milan Celeketic was appointed commander of the SVK by Milan Martic on the 22nd of February, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Rule 65 ter number 06123 , please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The document that is on the screen, is that the degree appointing Milan Celeketic?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, can that be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P171, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: After Celeketic, do you know who took over?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: A new commander was pointed in 1995, toward the middle of 1995, General Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, I now want to turn your attention to dealing with the Bosnian Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And I want to take you back to 1990. What was the position of the Bosnian Serbs at the founding assembly of the political party, the Serbian political party in Bosnia and Herzegovina? And if I could have on the screen Rule 65 ter number 06696, please.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I take it you're referring to the position they adopted on some of the current issues of the day.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If we can see that --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That's on page 3.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- in this document. This document is a speech given by Radovan Karadzic at the founding assembly of the Serbian Democratic Party of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which is a different party than the Serbian Democratic Party in Croatia. In this speech he indicates some of the objectives of that party and the same assembly on the same day elected him president of the party and adopted the party programme and statutes which reflect what he says here. If I can draw the Court's attention to the bottom half of page 3, in the paragraph beginning with: "The basic objective of the party is full and unconditional civil, national, cultural, religious, and economic equality for the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Here we cannot have peoples who lead or follow, first or second-rate citizens, nation-building and non-nation-building elements. "The objective of the party is to improve multi-national relations, establish stability and reciprocity, enhance civilian tranquility. "The objective of the party is Federative Yugoslavia consisting of an equal federal Bosnia-Herzegovina. Should this objective not be attainable, the party will strive to facility democratic methods including those which will enable the Serbian people to respond to a new situation." So the Serbian Democratic Party of Bosnia and Herzegovina also wished for the Serbs in their republic to remain within Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, can that document be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is so admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P172, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And what was the Bosnian Serb's position by the end of 1990? Did it change in any way?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could we have Rule 65 ter number 06675 on the screen, please, page 4.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they maintained that position.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What is this document, Mr. Treanor?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is -- this document is the transcript of an audio and sound recording that was made of a meeting held in Banja Luka on the 13th of October, 1990, at a time when elections, the multi-party elections had already been scheduled in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Elections that the SDS in BH were going to take part and at this meeting, a Serbian National Council for BH was founded.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Who was on that council?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The council included leaders of the Serbian Democratic Party, and Radovan Karadzic was the president of the council.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And what -- what position were they taking in October 1990, in relation to boundaries, state boundaries?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I think -- to answer that question, I think I can direct you to -- I'm sorry, I'm still looking at the original here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could perhaps go to the middle of the page?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's page 4 of the translation. Here Radovan Karadzic addresses the issue of borders. He says: "They have changed the concept of borders. Change of quality and nature of our internal borders. So the administrative lines that supposedly connect us have been transformed or will soon be transformed into hard state borders which divide us. These gentlemen care about the shape of the borders if it runs along this or that bank of a river or side of the meadow. They don't care to preserve the nature of these borders which are internal administrative lines between brotherly nations. One should know that most of these future hard borders are supposed to cut through the living tissue of Serbian people. They would like to cut and divide Serbian people against Serbian people's will. Hatred against Serbs and Serbia has not been developed by accident. This was a well-designed and carefully executed plan." The reference to the borders is to the existing borders of the republics of the former Yugoslavia which were of course not international borders; they were internal borders, and Radovan Karadzic is here objecting to their being changed into international borders by the recognition of the independence of individual republics, which as we've discussed, was something that for instance Croatia was moving toward and this was something that as we've seen that Slobodan Milosevic was objecting to.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, can I direct your attention to the bottom of page 5 of the English translation. What was the point that -- that Radovan Karadzic was making there?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, here he is reemphasizing the idea that the Serbs in Serbia want to remain in one state with Serbia. At the very bottom of the page he says: "But this did not help us in achieving constitutional guarantees for federation and founding an assembly of nations. Serbian people in BH will not give up their demands to live in one same state with our parent country, Serbia." And just below that, on top of the next page, where that passage ends, at the top of the page, after an interruption.

utterances.speaker: DR. KARADZIC SAYS
utterances.text: "Nobody can confederalise us against our will. Here today with your consent we will form the Serbian National Council of BiH." Here we see him objecting to the idea of confederalisation, which is something we have seen that Slobodan Milosevic was also objecting to.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: We can see the decision was then taken on forming the national -- the Serbian National Council. I can direct you to the bottom of the… that page 6. What was the outcome of the decision of the Serbian National Council?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They took a decision along the lines that he had been referred to remaining in one country, stating that the decision was adopted pursuant to this decision by the Serbian National Council of BiH: "Serbian people in BiH will not accept any decisions altering the character of the BiH state except for a decision which would be reached on a referendum of Serbian people." So here we see a reference to the idea of a referendum of the Serbian people. Again, something that Slobodan Milosevic had advocated. We had seen a referendum of people by republics, and the reference to not accepting decisions is a reference to any decision that the assembly of BiH may pass, regarding the independence of Bosnia, which would separate the Serbs from Serbia. The Serbian people would not accept that without having their own referendum.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, may that document be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is so admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be Exhibit P173, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. P173.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Leading up to the November 1990 elections what if anything was intimated to happen if decisions altering the character of Bosnia-Herzegovina were adopted.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And if we could have Exhibit number, Rule 65 ter 06716 on the screen, please. On page 3 of the English translation and page 2 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What was the position of the Bosnian Serbs, if -- if there were any decisions altering the character of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in this interview Radovan Karadzic makes reference to the situation that could develop as he puts it in the passage at the bottom of page 3, the paragraph beginning: "Without the Chamber of peoples."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry may I interrupt you. What is this document?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry. This document is an interview with Radovan Karadzic that was published in November 1991, on the 9th of November, 1991, in the Belgrade news magazine, Nin. And this paragraph in discussing that issue, he makes references to a Chambers of peoples. At the beginning of the paragraph what the discussion here refers to is the idea that the Serbs or the Serbian representatives in the assembly which was about to be elected. This is just before the elections, could be outvoted by the representatives, the deputies who were members of other nations in a simple majority vote. This was something that they did not -- the Serbian leaders, the Bosnian Serb leaders did not want to see happen, and they had suggested that a new chamber in the assembly be created called the Chamber of peoples in which the representatives of any particular people would be able to block any measure in the assembly that they felt threatened the vital interests of their people. That the SDS had suggested that to the existing assembly, the outgoing assembly, in November in a letter, it doesn't draw any -- it didn't happen at that time, let me put it that way, and that's what the reference is to here, his fear of being outvoted on the question of independence in the assembly. He says: "The BH assembly could become a place of dramatic events because the Serbs could be outvoted by a two-thirds majority regarding for instance the change of the state character of BH. Should that happen all conditions for a civil war would be in place because the Serbs in BH are no longer helpless but very powerful and united."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, can that document be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is so admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P174, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, briefly, what happened as a result of the November 1990 elections?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And if I could Rule 65 ter number 02232 on the screen, please, at page 2 of the English translation and page 4 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the elections were held later in November at various levels in the republic. That is there were elections for republic level posts as well as for municipal level posts. On the federal level, the elections were for the two Chambers, two existing Chambers of the assembly of BH and for the Presidency of BH. As a result of those elections, the SDS won 72 seats in the combined in the two houses, the two houses of the BH assembly, which was -- the total number is important because the assembly sometimes met in joint session to consider particularly important issues. The party for democratic action, which was basically a Muslim party won 80-some odd seats, and the HDZ in Croatia won a smaller number of seats, each of those parties won a number of seats in the assembly roughly proportionate to the representation of their respective nationalities in the population of BH. The Croats representing about 20 per cent, the Serbs 30 per cent, and the Muslims 43 per cent. They were all anti-Communist parties, and they had been afraid that the Communists were going to rig the elections somehow and so they cooperated to a certain extent before the elections and they in fact formed a coalition government after the elections; and they also came to an agreement on the division of power in the municipalities as well. So as a result of the elections the SDS entered a coalition government at the republic level and won a majority in a -- an outright majority in a sizeable number of municipalities in Bosnia and participated in government in many other municipalities where it was cooperating with the other parties. So it came out of the elections with a very strong political position within the republic. As a result of the agreement among the parties, the position of president of the assembly was allotted to the SDS; and Momcilo Krajisnik became the president of the assembly, and the Presidency, two Serbs backed by the SDS were elected, so two of the seven members of the Presidency were SDS people. Not necessarily members of the party but had been supported by them in the government the SDS received a number of ministries but not the position of prime minister, which went to the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor I think we have to stop there. We'll come back to that document tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I note the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. Because of the latest of the hour, we have to adjourn. Tomorrow we are not sitting.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry, Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So we will adjourn to Thursday, at quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon, same courtroom. Am I right? Yes, Courtroom II, quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon, Thursday, the 6th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 6th day of November, 2008, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.02 p.m.,
